newsitem.title: CHINA: Cambodia's King Sihanouk says ready to step down.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's King Sihanouk says ready to step down.

text.p: Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk has said he is ready to abdicate as soon as he is sure that the country's leader, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, will not criticise him for doing so.
"I am ready to abdicate as soon as it will be possible for me to do so," Sihanouk wrote in a private letter to his biographer sent to news agencies on Monday.
"My letter of abdication... has already been drafted by me for more than one week," Sihanouk wrote.

He said he was only waiting for signals or assurances from Hun Sen that he could abdicate without risk of being criticised by him or being accused of exacerbating the difficulties of the Cambodian people.
Sihanouk, a constitutional monarch who reigns but does not rule, said he would hold a private meeting with Hun Sen and his new co-premier Ung Huot on Tuesday morning at his residence in Beijing.
Hun Sen and Ung Huot are due to arrive on Monday in the Chinese capital, where Sihanouk is receiving medical treatment, to seek his political blessing.
"Our meeting will be of private and non-political nature," Sihanouk said in a faxed statement.
Hun Sen toppled his original co-premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, Sihanouk's son, last month. The king's approval is the last hurdle in his push to legitimise his power-grab.

Sihanouk has not tried to block Hun Sen since he seized sole power. He has said acting head of state Chea Sim could sign decrees on the king's behalf, including the appointment of Foreign Minister Ung Huot as first premier in place of Ranariddh.
However Sihanouk has indicated his disapproval of the political upheavals, saying in comments issued late last week that he still recognised Ranariddh as first prime minister.
"I have to say that we have three prime ministers -- one in forced exile, one a "puppet" and the real master of Cambodia today," he said.
"This is a 'fait accompli' that I cannot ignore," he said.

Political analysts in Cambodia say Hun Sen, who needs the king's blessing to consolidate his position domestically and internationally, might not get what he wants in his first meeting with Sihanouk since his coup.
"Sihanouk is the last step for Hun Sen. He has to get that legitimacy but he's hitting a brick wall and that's the king," said one analyst.
The king has said he would not be a player in his country's current political "comedy" because his views differed radically from those of the people in power. He said he was powerless to intervene.
The king is still revered by many Cambodians, and diplomats said one of Hun Sen's biggest worries is that Sihanouk will return to Cambodia and challenge him for power.
